course.name: Responsible Data Science: Privacy, Fairness and Documentation

los.description: Distinguish pseudonymisation, de-identification, aggregation, synthetic data and differential privacy by the guarantee and cost of each, given five described data releases
Measure re-identification risk from quasi-identifiers and reduce it while tracking analytic utility, given 60,000 synthetic applicant records and a linkable external file
Compute differentially private counts and means and state the accuracy cost of a privacy budget, given three candidate budgets
Test a synthetic extract for analytic utility and membership-inference leakage, given a generator trained on the applicant table
Audit a screening model for subgroup disparities, choose fairness criteria that fit the decision and evaluate two mitigations, given a scored test set with protected and intersectional attributes
Build the datasheet, model card and impact assessment a reviewer needs to judge and rerun a release, given the participant's capstone release

questions.prompt: Malak replaces each national identifier with its SHA-256 hash and removes names. Birth date, gender and postcode stay. Waad says the extract is now anonymous. What do you answer?
options: Yes: a hash cannot be reversed, so nobody can find the person
No: the hash is a pseudonym and the quasi-identifiers still single people out
Yes, as long as it stays on the university's servers
No, but only because names were in the original table
questions.explanation: Hashing is pseudonymisation: recomputable by anyone with the identifiers, and it leaves birth date, gender and postcode, which together are unique for almost every applicant.
misconceptions: Treats a one-way function as a missing key: anyone with the list of identifiers recomputes the same hashes
Confuses who holds the data with what the data is: the extract identifies people wherever it sits
Thinks names are the only identifier: birth date, gender and postcode do the identifying here

questions.prompt: Bashayer wants applicants per district on a public dashboard, refreshed every month. Some districts have fewer than ten applicants a month. Which control fits best?
options: Pseudonymise the applicant numbers before counting
Suppress every count below ten each month
Publish a synthetic extract instead of counts
Add calibrated noise under a stated yearly privacy budget
questions.explanation: Differential privacy bounds what any one applicant changes in every release, and the budget makes the cost of monthly repetition explicit.
misconceptions: Thinks a code protects published numbers: pseudonymisation applies to rows, not to counts
Assumes suppression is free when repeated: monthly tables with suppressed cells can be differenced against each other
Uses a row-level control for an aggregate need, and gives up the counts the dashboard is for

questions.prompt: Release A links 99% of the register's applicants on birth date, gender and postcode. Waad needs household size and approval by region. Which single change cuts the links most while keeping her question answerable?
options: Replace the birth date with an age band
Remove gender
Replace the study code with a new random code
Round income to the nearest 1,000 riyals
questions.explanation: The birth date has by far the most values of the three fields; coarsening it collapses the combinations, and the question needs only an age band.
misconceptions: Removes a field that has only two values: gender splits each class in half and barely changes uniqueness
Thinks the code is what links: the study code was never part of the join
Protects a sensitive attribute, not an identifier: linkage uses the quasi-identifiers, not the income

questions.prompt: Release B and release C both have k = 1. B has 2,152 unique records and C has 7. Yahya asks whether they are equally risky. What do you tell him?
options: Yes: both have k = 1, so both expose someone
B is safer because its birth year and district are more precise
C is far safer, but neither meets k of five until the small classes are treated
C is safe to release as it is, since seven records is negligible
questions.explanation: k reports only the worst class. The count of unique records and the average risk show that C exposes 7 people and B exposes 2,152, yet both still fail the target.
misconceptions: Reads k as the whole story: k is only the smallest class, so it hides how many people are exposed
Confuses detail kept for the analysis with protection: finer birth and place values split classes and raise the risk
Treats seven people as negligible: each of them is certainly re-identified by anyone who knows them

questions.prompt: Yesterday three fields linked 99.2% of the register's applicants to their income and decision. Yahya asks what the attacker had to have. Which answer is right?
options: The key that maps study codes back to applicants
At least one direct identifier left in the release
An outside file sharing birth date, gender and postcode with the release
The applicants' incomes, to match them to the release
questions.explanation: A linkage attack needs only quasi-identifiers that an outside file shares with the release; the names come from the outside file.
misconceptions: Assumes re-identification needs the fund's secrets: the study code was never used in the join
Thinks only direct identifiers re-identify: no name or national identifier was in the release
Confuses the harm with the means: income is what the link revealed, not what it used

questions.prompt: At five-year band and district, 1,728 records (2.9%) are below five. Waad wants to keep the district. Malak can suppress those 1,728 or move to region and suppress 293. What should she weigh?
options: Which small groups the 1,728 are, and whether Waad's question needs the district
Always the option with fewer suppressed records
Always suppression, since it leaves every kept record exact
Whichever option gives the higher k
questions.explanation: Both meet k of five. The choice is about utility: what the question needs, and whose records the suppression removes.
misconceptions: Thinks the least suppression always wins: it ignores what the question needs
Thinks suppression is free because rows are simply removed: they are the rare groups, so estimates for them shift
Confuses the target with a preference: k of five is met either way, so k cannot decide it

questions.prompt: Malak releases the 59 district counts at epsilon 0.1 instead of 0.5. Bashayer asks what changed. Which statement is right?
options: The large districts now carry most of the error
The counts are now private, where before they were not
The noise is 59 times larger, one share per district
Each count's noise is about five times larger, and the guarantee is stronger
questions.explanation: The scale is sensitivity over epsilon: going from 0.5 to 0.1 multiplies it by five, and a smaller epsilon bounds any one applicant's influence more tightly.
misconceptions: Thinks noise grows with the count: the noise scale is set by sensitivity and epsilon, not by the district's size
Thinks privacy is binary: every epsilon gives a guarantee, a smaller one is a stronger one
Confuses the sensitivity with the number of counts: one person changes one count, whatever the number of districts

questions.prompt: Malak releases applicants per region, 13 counts, each with noise of scale 10 (epsilon 0.1 for a count). Every applicant is in exactly one region. What has the release spent?
options: 1.3, the sum over the 13 regions
0.1, because the regions hold disjoint applicants
About 0.008, a thirteenth of 0.1
Nothing, since counts are aggregates
questions.explanation: Parallel composition: one applicant affects only one region's count, so the release spends the epsilon of one count.
misconceptions: Adds epsilons over disjoint groups: sequential composition applies only to releases about the same people
Divides the budget instead of adding it: splitting into regions does not make each count cheaper
Thinks counts are free because they are aggregates: every noisy count spends budget

questions.prompt: A vendor's synthetic file matches the real one on utility. No row is an exact copy, and 31% of its rows are closer to the training data than to a holdout. What do you conclude?
options: Nothing blocks it on these tests: no copies, and no preference for training rows
It leaks: 31% of rows sit next to training records
It is too accurate to be private, so it must be copying
It is differentially private, since no row is copied
questions.explanation: Leakage shows as more closeness to training rows than to unseen rows. 31% is below the 50% of no preference, and no row is copied.
misconceptions: Reads any share below 100% as leakage: the warning sign is a share well above 50%, not below it
Treats high utility as a leak in itself: utility is a warning only when copies or membership show memorising
Thinks no copies means a formal guarantee: these tests are evidence against one attack, not a proof

questions.prompt: Bashayer approves the district counts at epsilon 0.5 and asks for them every month. Yahya asks what the fund will have spent after a year.
options: 0.5, because each month is a separate table
6, because the same applicants are counted twelve times
0.5, because later months are post-processing
About 0.04, a twelfth of 0.5
questions.explanation: Sequential composition: twelve releases about the same people spend twelve times 0.5.
misconceptions: Applies parallel composition across months: the months are about the same applicants, so the epsilons add
Thinks post-processing covers new releases: each month is a new measurement on the data, not a computation on last month's output
Divides instead of adding: splitting a budget into months is a choice, not what happens by default

questions.prompt: Hail has an FNR of 18.2% from 110 eligible applicants, interval 12.1% to 26.4%. The FNR over all 6,341 eligible applicants is 22.8%. Wiam asks whether Ahliya treats Hail's applicants better.
options: Yes: 18.2% is lower than 22.8%, so Hail is treated better
Nothing at all, since 110 applicants is too few to compute a rate
No difference is shown: the interval includes the overall rate
No: small regions are always disadvantaged by the model
questions.explanation: The interval from 12.1% to 26.4% contains 22.8%, so the data do not show that Hail differs.
misconceptions: Reads a point estimate without its interval: the interval includes the overall rate
Treats a wide interval as no information: it still rules out very high or very low rates
Confuses a smaller group with a worse outcome: size widens the interval, it does not move the rate

questions.prompt: Ahliya decides who is passed to an officer for housing support. Eligible applicants are more common among women. Bashayer asks which fairness criterion the fund should commit to.
options: Equal false negative rates: miss eligible applicants equally in each group
Equal selection rates: pass the same share of women and men
All three criteria at once, to be safe
None: Ahliya does not use gender, so it is fair
questions.explanation: The harmful error in a support decision is the missed eligible applicant, and need differs between groups, so error rates among the eligible are what must be equal.
misconceptions: Ignores the different need: equal selection would decline eligible women to match men's rate
Thinks all criteria can be met together: with different base rates they conflict
Equates removing an input with fair outcomes: outcomes still differ through other features

questions.prompt: Self-employed applicants are missed by Ahliya far more often. An income audit shows their recorded income is 1.73 times the verified income; for employees it is 1.00. Which type fits, and what is the first fix?
options: Labeling Bias: retrain on corrected decisions
Sampling Bias: reweight the self-employed in training
Historical Bias: retrain on recent applications only
Measurement Bias: record net income for the self-employed
questions.explanation: The feature itself is systematically over-recorded for one group, which is the guide's measurement bias; the fix is at the point of recording.
misconceptions: Blames the outcome when the evidence points at a feature: the officers applied the rule correctly to the income they were given
Reaches for a mitigation that cannot repair a wrong input: weights change counts, not recorded incomes
Treats every old pattern as historical: nothing here changed over time

questions.prompt: Reweighting moved the FNR gap from 12.9 to 12.6 points. Group thresholds moved it to 10.0, at the same accuracy. The gap comes mostly from missing and mis-recorded income. What do you recommend to Bashayer?
options: Group thresholds as the permanent fix, since accuracy did not fall
Fix income recording first; thresholds only as an approved interim measure
Reweighting, because pre-processing is always preferable
Neither, since the gap is not closed completely
questions.explanation: The cause is in the income feature, so the lasting fix is at the source; the threshold change helps meanwhile but needs approval because it uses gender and nationality.
misconceptions: Reads an unchanged accuracy as a free fix: the rule uses protected attributes and the gap remains
Ignores what the evidence showed: the weights cannot repair a wrong feature
Treats an unfinished fix as no fix: a narrowed gap with monitoring is better than the baseline

questions.prompt: Anmar reports that eligible women and men are missed at 22.7% and 22.8%. He proposes to close the audit.
options: Not shown: the intersection of gender and nationality must be checked too
Yes: equal false negative rates by gender meet equal opportunity
No: the selection rates by gender must also be equal
Not until every region by gender by nationality cell is estimated
questions.explanation: Non-Saudi women are missed at 29.8%, which the gender margin hides.
misconceptions: Reads equal margins as equal treatment: a gap inside an intersection can cancel out in both margins
Moves to a criterion the course did not choose: for support by need, the harm is the missed eligible applicant
Treats every slice as required: cells below the minimum of 30 eligible are reported as too few, not audited

questions.prompt: Malak's draft says: "k = 5 was reached, so the extract is anonymous and no risk remains." Yahya sends it back.
options: That k should be raised to 10 before release
That the sharing agreement makes residual risk irrelevant
That 99.2% of applicants can still be linked
The risks k does not cover, and that the extract is still personal data
questions.explanation: k limits singling out on the chosen quasi-identifiers only; attribute disclosure and other files remain, and the data stay Restricted.
misconceptions: Moves the problem to a number: a larger k narrows linkage risk but still says nothing about classes that share one value
Confuses documentation with access control: the agreement limits use, it does not remove the risk the datasheet must state
Reports the before-treatment figure as if it remained: no register record matched one record after treatment

questions.prompt: Anmar's card has all seven sections. Its results table shows gender and region, each with intervals. Wiam rejects it.
options: The card omits the validation report's 88.1%
It does not estimate every region by gender cell
It hides the largest gap, which is in gender by nationality
The gap is not closed, so the card cannot be filed
questions.explanation: Non-Saudi women are missed at 29.8%; margins by gender and region alone do not show it.
misconceptions: Asks for a figure the card already handles: the vendor's number is named and explained, not required
Asks for more rows than the data support: small cells are reported as too few, not filled
Reads the absence of a fix as a defect of the card: the card records the mitigation, it does not have to close the gap

questions.prompt: Malak scores R2's likelihood as 2, "unlikely", because officers can overturn Ahliya. The audit measured 1,444 of 6,341 eligible applicants declined by the screen.
options: 2 is right, since officers review every decision
4: the harm is measured now, without an effective control
3, so that the level does not reach the catastrophic band
1, because the gender gap is only 0.1 points
questions.explanation: Likelihood is argued from exposure and the controls in place; the harm is already measured and auto-declines bypass review.
misconceptions: Counts a control that is not in place: 37.4% of applications are auto-declined and never seen by an officer
Lowers the likelihood because the impact is high: the two scores are argued separately
Scores on fairness instead of harm: likelihood asks how probable the harm is, not whether groups differ

questions.prompt: A peer reports an FNR gap of -2.9 points; your rerun on all rows at 0.5 gives -0.2. The bootstrap is unseeded, the threshold is 0.45, and 633 rows with missing income are dropped.
options: The dropped rows: removing them alone takes the gap from +0.6 to -2.9
The unseeded bootstrap, because each run differs
The threshold of 0.45, because it differs from the documented 0.5
A different pandas version on the peer's machine
questions.explanation: At the peer's threshold, keeping the rows gives +0.6; dropping them gives -2.9, because they are mostly women Ahliya misses.
misconceptions: Blames the visible randomness: an unseeded bootstrap moves the interval, not the point estimate
Picks the documented mismatch: at all rows, 0.45 against 0.5 moves the gap by under one point
Assumes environments explain differences: the same code on the same data reproduced the claim exactly

questions.prompt: Yusr replaces each national identifier in a research extract with a salted hash. The data protection officer keeps the salt. The researcher asks whether the extract is still personal data.
options: No: the recipient cannot reverse a salted hash
Yes: the fund can relink it, so it is still personal data
No: once direct identifiers are gone the data are anonymous
Only if the hash had been computed without a salt
questions.explanation: Pseudonymised data can be linked back with information the fund holds, so the national anonymisation guideline treats it as personal data.
misconceptions: Treats one-way hashing as anonymisation; the fund can still relink, and other fields still single people out
Ignores both the key the fund keeps and the quasi-identifiers left in the rows
Thinks the salt changes the legal status; it slows guessing, it does not stop the fund relinking

questions.prompt: The board wants to publish approved applications per district each quarter, including districts with fewer than ten applicants. Which control fits, and what does it cost?
options: Differential privacy; small districts get noisier figures
Pseudonymisation of the counts; nothing is lost
k-anonymity on the published table; rows can still be linked
A synthetic copy of the table; the counts stay exact
questions.explanation: Counts are aggregates; differential privacy bounds what one applicant changes, and the price is noise that matters most where counts are small.
misconceptions: Applies a record-level control to a table of counts, where there is no identifier to replace
Applies a microdata control to aggregates, and misstates what it leaves behind
Expects exact counts from synthetic data, which neither keeps them exact nor bounds the risk

questions.prompt: A university requests an extract of 40,000 applicants with region, five-year age band, household size and support status, treated to k = 5. Under the Data Classification Policy, at what level does it stay?
options: Public, because k = 5 makes it anonymous
Secret, because it concerns social support
No level, because de-identified data are outside the policy
Restricted, as personal data about individuals
questions.explanation: The policy lists personal data under Restricted; de-identification lowers the risk but the extract remains personal data.
misconceptions: Thinks a treatment changes the class; it lowers the risk of the data, which are still about people
Over-classifies: the harm of disclosure does not reach the level the Secret class describes
Thinks some data escape classification; every data asset gets a level

questions.prompt: A university researcher emails Yusr directly to ask for applicant records for her study. Under the General Rules for Secondary Use of Data, what is missing?
options: Nothing: research is a legitimate purpose, so her email request is enough
A public release of the records first, so that anyone may use them
A request via her institution with written approval, for minimum data
Only encryption of the file when it is sent
questions.explanation: The rules route a researcher's request through her institution with written approval, and limit the data to what the purpose needs.
misconceptions: Takes a legitimate purpose as the only condition; the route and the minimum data matter too
Confuses secondary use under conditions with open data
Treats a transfer safeguard as the permission to use the data

questions.prompt: Release A drops names and national identifiers but keeps birth date, gender and postcode. A public register lists names with the same three fields. A join re-identifies 99.2% of the register's applicants. Why?
options: Together the three fields are unique for almost everyone
The register also holds the applicants' national identifiers
The postcode alone points to one applicant
The test must be wrong, since linkage needs exact names
questions.explanation: Birth date, gender and postcode in combination single out almost everyone, so a join on them finds one match per person.
misconceptions: Assumes the attack needs an identifier; it joined on the quasi-identifiers only
Credits a single field; it is the combination that is unique
Denies the result; linkage needs shared fields, not names

questions.prompt: In candidate release B, 2,152 records are unique on the quasi-identifiers. What is k for release B, and what does it say?
options: k = 2,152: the number of records at risk
k = 1: at least one record can be singled out on these fields
k is unknown until a linkage test is run
k = 1, so every single record in release B is unique
questions.explanation: k is the size of the smallest equivalence class; a unique record is a class of one.
misconceptions: Confuses k with a count of unique records
Thinks k needs an outside file; it is computed from the release alone
Reads k, a minimum, as a statement about every class

questions.prompt: To reach k = 5, node (a) uses five-year birth bands and region and suppresses 293 records; node (b) uses ten-year bands and region and suppresses 84. The study asks how approval varies with age. What do you choose and report?
options: (b), because fewer suppressed records always means more utility
(a), without mentioning the suppressed records, since k is met
Neither: k = 5 needs the age field removed entirely
(a), reporting the suppressed records and the change by age
questions.explanation: The research question needs age detail, and a release reports both its suppression and its measured utility change.
misconceptions: Counts only one cost; ten-year bands blur the age effect the study needs
Hides who was removed, which can bias the analysis
Contradicted by both nodes, which reach k = 5 with age kept

questions.prompt: After treatment k = 5, but in one class all five records have disability in household = yes. A recipient knows her neighbour is in that class. What has the treatment failed to prevent?
options: Identity disclosure: she can now find her neighbour's exact record
Nothing, since k = 5 protects every attribute
Attribute disclosure: she learns the status without the record
Membership inference, which arises only in synthetic data
questions.explanation: When a class shares one sensitive value, membership in the class reveals it; k does not prevent this.
misconceptions: Forgets that k = 5 leaves five candidates for one person
Reads k as a guarantee about attributes, which it does not give
Names a different attack from another release type

questions.prompt: Yusr releases district counts with differential privacy at epsilon 0.5. What does this promise each applicant?
options: Their record is removed from the data before the counts are made
No count is off by more than 0.5
No one can learn anything about their district
The counts are almost as likely with or without their record
questions.explanation: Differential privacy bounds how much any one record can change the probability of the output.
misconceptions: Confuses differential privacy with suppression
Reads epsilon as a bound on the error
Expects protection of group facts; the guarantee is about one person's record

questions.prompt: A count per district is released with the Laplace mechanism. Each applicant is in exactly one district. At epsilon 0.5, what is the noise scale?
options: 0.5: the scale equals epsilon
2: sensitivity 1 divided by epsilon 0.5
1: the scale equals the sensitivity
0.25: sensitivity times epsilon
questions.explanation: The Laplace scale is sensitivity divided by epsilon; one applicant changes one count by 1.
misconceptions: Uses epsilon as the scale; a smaller epsilon must mean more noise, not less
Leaves epsilon out of the scale
Multiplies, which would add less noise for stronger privacy

questions.prompt: Over a year the fund releases four tables about the same applicants at epsilon 0.1, 0.2, 0.2 and 0.5. What is the total privacy loss?
options: 1.0: releases about the same people add up
0.5: the largest of the four
0.25: their average
0.1: the smallest, because it protects the most
questions.explanation: Under sequential composition, releases about the same people spend the sum of their epsilons.
misconceptions: Applies the parallel rule, which holds only for disjoint groups of people
Averages losses that accumulate
Thinks the strongest release covers the others

questions.prompt: District counts at epsilon 0.1, 0.5 and 1 give a mean error of 9.98, 1.92 and 0.85, and a relative error in the ten smallest districts of 16%, 3.1% and 1.5%. The dashboard must keep small districts within about 5%. Which budget do you recommend?
options: 0.1, because the smallest budget is always the safest choice
1, because its error is the lowest
0.5: the smallest budget that meets the need in small districts
Any of them, since all mean errors are below 10
questions.explanation: Choose the smallest epsilon whose error meets the use, measured where the error matters most.
misconceptions: Ignores fitness for use: 16% error in small districts misleads readers
Spends more privacy than the stated need requires
Judges by the average, which hides the small districts

questions.prompt: Bashayer says: "The hackathon file is synthetic, so no applicant can be in it." What do you answer?
options: She is right: synthetic rows are invented by definition
A generator can copy training rows, so leakage is tested first
She is right if the file has as many rows as the original
Only a differentially private generator may ever be released at all
questions.explanation: A flexible generator can memorise its training data, so copying and membership inference are tested before release.
misconceptions: Assumes a generator cannot reproduce its training rows
Links privacy to the number of rows, which says nothing about copying
Overcorrects: measured leakage tests are another accepted basis for release

questions.prompt: 0.10% of synthetic rows match a training record exactly, and 0.05% match a record from a holdout the generator never saw. What does this suggest?
options: The file leaks, because any exact copy is a leak
The holdout comparison means nothing, since the generator never saw it
Utility is too low, because so few rows match real ones
Copies are close to the rate of chance matches seen on the holdout
questions.explanation: Rows the generator never saw are matched almost as often, so most matches are coincidences of common values, not memorisation.
misconceptions: Ignores matches by coincidence, which the holdout measures
Misses that the unseen holdout is the baseline for chance matches
Confuses copying with utility, which is measured on analyses

questions.prompt: A membership-inference test gives AUC 0.819 for a generator with leaves of one row, and 0.511 with leaves of 200 rows. What do you conclude?
options: With leaves of 200, an attacker does little better than chance
Leaves of one are better, since a higher AUC means more utility
Neither can be released, since any AUC above 0.5 is leakage
Nothing, since AUC measures the attack, not the file
questions.explanation: An AUC near 0.5 means the attacker cannot tell training rows from others; 0.819 means it often can.
misconceptions: Reads the attack's AUC as if it were a model's accuracy
Treats a value within noise of 0.5 as evidence of leakage
Misses that the attack's success is the measure of the file's leakage

questions.prompt: The leaf-200 file copies 0.10% of rows (holdout 0.05%), membership AUC 0.511, and a model trained on it reaches AUC 0.933 against 0.936 on real data. The hackathon will train models. What do you recommend?
options: Release the leaf-one file, which reproduces the real data more closely
Release this file and stop running the tests, since they passed once
Release this file with its leakage tests and generator settings documented
Hold it until its utility matches the real data exactly
questions.explanation: Utility is close to real and leakage is at chance, so release with the evidence documented.
misconceptions: Prefers fidelity over privacy; that file copied 92.8% of rows
Forgets that every regeneration needs the same release gate
Asks for perfect utility, which only copying achieves

questions.prompt: In Al-Jouf, 4 non-Saudi women were eligible and the screen declined 3. How should the audit report this cell?
options: As a false negative rate of 75%, the highest in the audit
As too few to estimate, with the count of 4
Merged with Saudi women in Al-Jouf, without saying so
Not at all: the region is dropped from the report
questions.explanation: Below the minimum count the rate is not estimated; the count is reported so the reader sees why.
misconceptions: Reports a rate from four people as if it were precise
Changes the slice silently, which hides a choice from the reader
Removes evidence instead of stating its limit

questions.prompt: Forcing equal selection rates for women and men opened a 12.4-point gap in their false negative rates. For a decision on housing support, which criterion fits?
options: Equal false negative rates: the harm is missing eligible people
Equal selection rates, which is what fairness means
Equal precision, since every approved applicant must be eligible
All three at once, by tuning the threshold carefully
questions.explanation: Equal opportunity fits a support decision: the error that harms is missing an eligible applicant.
misconceptions: Treats one criterion as the definition, regardless of the decision
Puts the fund's cost of wrong approvals before the applicant's harm
Different base rates make the criteria conflict; no threshold meets all three

questions.prompt: Self-employed applicants' recorded income is 1.5 to 2 times their verified income, and the screen declines more than half of the eligible self-employed. Which bias type of the national AI Bias Reference Guide does this match?
options: Historical bias
Sampling bias
Feedback loop bias
Measurement bias
questions.explanation: A feature that records the quantity wrongly for one group is measurement bias.
misconceptions: The past rule is a different finding; here the field itself is wrong
The self-employed are in the data; it is their values that are off
Describes retraining on the model's own outcomes, not a recorded value

questions.prompt: Group thresholds narrow the false negative gap from 12.9 to 10.0 points at the same accuracy. What must accompany them before deployment?
options: Nothing, since accuracy did not fall
Reweighting first, since post-processing is not allowed
Approval to use gender and nationality, and an income fix
Removing gender and nationality, so the rule cannot be challenged
questions.explanation: The rule uses protected attributes at decision time, which needs approval, and the cause lies in the income feature.
misconceptions: Treats unchanged accuracy as the only cost
Invents a rule; reweighting barely helped here because the cause is a feature
Contradicts itself: the thresholds need those attributes

questions.prompt: Malak fills the datasheet's De-identification section from her notebook's last run, which suppressed 290 records. The release log says 293. What should she write?
options: 290, since it is the more recent run
293, the number in the log of the released run
291.5, the average, with a note on uncertainty
No number, since a difference of three does not matter
questions.explanation: The datasheet describes the release that left the fund, which the log recorded.
misconceptions: Documents a run that was not the one approved and released
Invents a number that no run produced
Drops a fact the reviewer needs to check the release

questions.prompt: The vendor reports 88.1% accuracy against officers' decisions in two regions; against the reviewed outcome of 12,000 applications it is 84.8%. What goes in the model card?
options: 88.1%, since it is the figure the model was approved on
Both, without comment, so readers choose
Neither, since accuracy says nothing about fairness
84.8%, and why the vendor's 88.1% is not used
questions.explanation: Accuracy belongs against the reviewed outcome; naming the other figure prevents confusion.
misconceptions: Repeats an evaluation the audit found biased
Leaves the reader to resolve a difference the author understands
Drops a metric the reviewer needs alongside the group results

questions.prompt: Risk R2 (wrongful declines) scores likelihood 4 and impact 3. After adding officer review of every decline, Anmar rescores it as likelihood 2 and impact 1. Wiam rejects the new impact. Why?
options: Review lowers the chance of a wrong decision, not the harm when one happens
A residual cannot be scored until the treatment has run for a year
A high risk can only be avoided, never mitigated
Likelihood can never fall after a measured harm
questions.explanation: Treatment here acts on likelihood; an applicant still wrongly declined is harmed as before.
misconceptions: Invents a waiting rule; residual risk is scored when the treatment is chosen
Forgets that mitigate is one of the framework's four treatments
Denies that a control changes how probable the harm is

questions.prompt: A peer's script reproduces their claimed gap exactly. Your review finds it drops 633 rows with missing income, 65% of them women, and the README does not say so. What do you record?
